lessons.title: Continuous and perfect tenses
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III (Class 5) — English Language; to be checked against the official syllabus
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use the present and past continuous.
Use the present perfect (have/has + past participle).
Choose the right tense with time words.
reviewNotes: Only the most common uses of each tense are taught; present perfect continuous is not covered.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Continuous tenses
blocks.md: The **present continuous** (am/is/are + -ing) shows something happening **now**: *Mama is cooking ndolé.* The **past continuous** (was/were + -ing) shows something that was **in progress** in the past: *The children were playing when it started to rain.*

blocks.caption: Three tenses and their forms.
blocks.alt: A table with present continuous (is cooking), past continuous (were playing) and present perfect (has finished) and their forms.

blocks.title: Present perfect
blocks.md: The **present perfect** (have/has + past participle) links the past with now: *I have finished my homework.* *She has lived in Limbe for five years.* Words used with it: **already, yet, just, ever, never, for, since**. The past participle of regular verbs ends in -ed; irregular ones must be learnt: *eaten, gone, seen, written, bought, taken*.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using the continuous with state verbs: *I am knowing the answer* is wrong; say *I know*.
- Using the present perfect with a finished time: not *I have seen him yesterday* but *I saw him yesterday*.
- Using the wrong participle: *has went* (correct: *has gone*).
- Forgetting the -ing form: *She is cook*.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Complete: 'Look! The boys ___ football in the yard.' (play)
steps: The word 'Look!' shows that it is happening now.
Present continuous: are playing.

blocks.title: Example 2
steps: The word 'already' goes with the present perfect.
have + past participle of eat: have eaten.

lessons.title: Concord: harder cases
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III (Class 5) — English Language; to be checked against the official syllabus
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use the right verb with each, every, either, neither and collective nouns.
Treat uncountable nouns correctly.
Correct longer concord mistakes.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Singular words
blocks.md: These words take a **singular verb**: **each, every, everyone, everybody, someone, nobody, either, neither**. *Each of the boys **has** a book. Everybody **is** here. Neither of them **was** late.* The verb agrees with *each / neither*, not with the plural word that follows.

blocks.caption: Subjects and the verbs they take.
blocks.alt: A table of subjects and verbs: each of the boys has; neither Ako nor Bih was; a number of pupils are; the news is; maize and beans are.

blocks.title: Other cases
blocks.md: Two subjects joined by **and** are plural: *Maize and beans **are** cheap.* **Uncountable nouns** such as *news, advice, information, furniture, water* take a singular verb: *The news **is** good.* **A number of** takes a plural verb (*A number of pupils **are** absent*), **the number of** takes a singular verb (*The number of pupils **is** 40*).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *Each of the girls have*: it must be *has*.
- *The news are*: *news* is singular.
- *Advices* or *informations*: these words have no plural.
- Following the word right before the verb: *The box of mangoes **is** heavy* (the subject is box).

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Choose: 'Each of the pupils (has / have) a pencil.'
steps: The subject is Each, which is singular.
So we use has.

blocks.title: Example 2
steps: News looks plural but is uncountable and singular.
The news is good.

lessons.title: Pronouns and determiners: who, which, whose, some, any, much, many
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III (Class 5) — English Language; to be checked against the official syllabus
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use the relative pronouns who, which and whose.
Use some, any, much, many, a few and a little correctly.
Join two sentences with a relative pronoun.
reviewNotes: 'Whom' is not taught at this level; check the syllabus.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Relative pronouns
blocks.md: A **relative pronoun** joins two ideas. **Who** is for people: *The girl **who** sings is my sister.* **Which** is for things and animals: *The book **which** I read was long.* **Whose** shows ownership: *The boy **whose** bag is lost is crying.*

blocks.caption: Relative pronouns and quantity words.
blocks.alt: A table of words: who for people, which for things, whose for the owner, much for uncountable, many for countable, with examples.

blocks.title: Quantity words
blocks.md: Use **many** and **a few** with **countable** nouns (*many books, a few eggs*). Use **much** and **a little** with **uncountable** nouns (*much water, a little rice*). **Some** is used in positive sentences (*I have some rice*); **any** is used in questions and negatives (*Do you have any rice? I don't have any.*).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *Much books* or *many water*: use **many books**, **much water**.
- *Who* for things: *the car who* is wrong; say **which**.
- *I don't have some money*: say **any money**.
- Mixing *a few* (some) and *few* (not many).

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Join: 'I met a boy. The boy lives in Bali.' using who.
steps: Both sentences are about the same boy: the second becomes a who-clause.
I met a boy who lives in Bali.
blocks.answer: I met a boy who lives in Bali.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Choose much or many: 'How ___ water do you need?'
steps: Water cannot be counted: it is uncountable.
We use much.

lessons.title: Adjectives and adverbs: degrees of comparison
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III (Class 5) — English Language; to be checked against the official syllabus
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Form comparatives and superlatives of adjectives and adverbs.
Use as ... as, than and the.
Choose between an adjective and an adverb.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Degrees
blocks.md: **Adjectives** have three degrees: **positive** (tall), **comparative** (taller than) and **superlative** (the tallest). Adverbs with -ly use *more / most*: *slowly - more slowly - most slowly*. Some are irregular: **good / well - better - best**, **bad / badly - worse - worst**, **far - farther - farthest**.

blocks.caption: Three degrees of an adjective and an adverb.
blocks.alt: A table with positive, comparative and superlative: slow, slower, slowest for the adjective and slowly, more slowly, most slowly for the adverb.

blocks.title: Equal and not equal
blocks.md: Use **as + adjective + as** for equality: *Ako is as tall as Bih.* Use **not as ... as** for a lower degree: *Fish is not as expensive as beef.* Use **than** after a comparative: *taller than*. Use **the** with a superlative: *the tallest*.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *Gooder, badder*: use better, worse.
- Using an adjective instead of an adverb: *She sings good* should be *She sings well*.
- Double comparison: *more better*.
- *The most tallest*: use only one superlative form.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Complete: 'This road is ____ than that one.' (long)
steps: Two roads are compared: the comparative is needed.
Long adds -er: longer.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Choose the right word: 'She sings (good / well).'
steps: The word describes the verb sings, so we need an adverb.
The adverb is well.

lessons.title: Conjunctions, sentences and clauses
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III (Class 5) — English Language; to be checked against the official syllabus
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Join sentences with and, but, because, so, if, although and when.
Tell statements, questions, commands and exclamations apart.
Tell simple, compound and complex sentences apart.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Conjunctions
blocks.md: A **conjunction** joins words or sentences: **and** (adds), **but** (contrast), **or** (choice), **because** (reason), **so** (result), **if** (condition), **although** (contrast), **when** (time). *I was tired **so** I slept. We stayed inside **because** it was raining.* A clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb.

blocks.caption: Conjunctions and what they show.
blocks.alt: A table of joining words: and for addition, but for contrast, because for reason, so for result, although for contrast and if for condition, each with an example sentence.

blocks.title: Kinds of sentences
blocks.md: A **statement** gives information. A **question** asks. A **command** tells someone to do something. An **exclamation** shows strong feeling (*What a big fish!*). A **simple** sentence has one clause; a **compound** sentence joins two clauses with *and, but, or, so*; a **complex** sentence has a main clause and a clause with *because, although, if, when*.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using **but** and **although** together: *Although it rained, but we played* is wrong.
- Using *because* and *so* together in the same sentence.
- Starting a sentence with *because* and not finishing it (a sentence needs a main clause).
- Forgetting the comma after a clause that starts with *although* or *if*.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Join with 'because': 'Ako was late. The bus broke down.'
steps: The second sentence is the reason for the first.
Ako was late because the bus broke down.
blocks.answer: Ako was late because the bus broke down.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: What kind of sentence is: 'Close the door, please.'?
steps: It tells someone to do something.
It is a command.

lessons.title: Direct and indirect (reported) speech
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III (Class 5) — English Language; to be checked against the official syllabus
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Write direct speech with quotation marks.
Change simple statements and questions to reported speech.
Change pronouns and tenses correctly.
reviewNotes: Back-shifting rules are given in their simplest form; exceptions (general truths) are not covered.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Direct and indirect speech
blocks.md: **Direct speech** gives the exact words of the speaker inside **quotation marks**: *Ako said, "I am tired."* **Indirect (reported) speech** tells what was said without the exact words: *Ako said that he was tired.* There are no quotation marks, and the pronouns and tenses change.

items.text: Indirect: Ako said that he was tired.
I becomes he; am becomes was

blocks.caption: From direct to indirect speech.
blocks.alt: Four boxes: direct speech Ako said I am tired; indirect speech Ako said that he was tired; I becomes he and am becomes was; quotation marks disappear.

blocks.title: How to change
blocks.md:
1. Remove the quotation marks and add **that**.
2. Change the **pronouns** (I - he/she, my - his/her, we - they).
3. Move the **tense one step back**: *am/is - was*, *are - were*, *play - played*, *will - would*, *can - could*.
4. Change the **time and place words** if needed: *today - that day, tomorrow - the next day, here - there*.

blocks.title: Questions and commands
blocks.md: A reported **question** keeps no question mark and the word order of a statement: *She asked, "Where do you live?"* becomes *She asked where I lived.* A reported **command** uses *to*: *The teacher said, "Sit down."* becomes *The teacher told us to sit down.*

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Keeping the pronoun *I* in the reported sentence.
- Keeping the question mark or quotation marks.
- Not moving the tense back: *Ako said that he is tired*.
- Using *if* wrongly: for a yes/no question use *if* or *whether*.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Change to reported speech: Mary said, "I like mangoes."
steps: Remove the quotation marks, add that, change I to she and like to liked.
Mary said that she liked mangoes.
blocks.answer: Mary said that she liked mangoes.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Change to direct speech: The teacher said that the test would start at nine.
steps: Use the exact words of the teacher: will instead of would, and quotation marks.
The teacher said, "The test will start at nine."
blocks.answer: The teacher said, "The test will start at nine."

lessons.title: Active and passive voice (introduction)
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III (Class 5) — English Language; to be checked against the official syllabus
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Tell an active sentence from a passive sentence.
Change simple active sentences into the passive.
Choose the right form of 'to be' and the past participle.
reviewNotes: Passive voice may belong to later classes; included as an introduction only (flag for the teacher to keep or drop).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Active and passive
blocks.md: In an **active** sentence the doer comes first: *The farmer **plants** the maize.* In a **passive** sentence the thing receiving the action comes first: *The maize **is planted** by the farmer.* The passive is formed with **am / is / are / was / were + past participle**.

items.text: Active: The farmer plants the maize.
Passive: The maize is planted by the farmer.
Use the passive when the doer is not important

blocks.caption: Active and passive.
blocks.alt: Four boxes: active, the farmer plants the maize; passive, the maize is planted by the farmer; the form is a part of to be plus the past participle; the passive is used when the doer is not important.

blocks.title: Changing to the passive
blocks.md:
1. Find the **object** of the active sentence (*the maize*): it becomes the new subject.
2. Use the correct form of **to be** in the same tense (*plants - is planted*; *planted - was planted*).
3. Add the **past participle**.
4. Add **by + the doer** if it is useful (*by the farmer*).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using the simple past participle wrongly: *was wrote* (correct: *was written*).
- Forgetting the verb *to be*: *The maize planted by the farmer*.
- Keeping the wrong tense: *The letter is written yesterday* (should be *was written*).
- Using the passive when the active is clearer.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Change to the passive: 'The girl sweeps the classroom.'
steps: Object: the classroom (new subject). Tense: present simple, so is + participle.
The classroom is swept by the girl.
blocks.answer: The classroom is swept by the girl.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Change to the passive: 'Mama cooked the ndolé.'
steps: Object: the ndolé. Tense: past simple, so was + participle.
The ndolé was cooked by Mama.
blocks.answer: The ndolé was cooked by Mama.
